items.followUp: Define static friction and state what happens to it as an applied force increases before motion begins.

rubric.why: Identifies limiting friction as the greatest value of static friction.
rubric.description: States that limiting friction is the maximum static friction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as the maximum static friction.

rubric.why: Shows the condition at which limiting friction acts.
rubric.description: States that it acts when the body is just about to move relative to the surface.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the impending-motion condition.

modelAnswer: Limiting friction is the maximum value of static friction acting between two surfaces when one body is just about to move over the other.

items.followUp: A car's velocity changes from 5 m/s to 17 m/s in 4 s. Find its acceleration and write the SI unit.

rubric.why: Gives the defining relationship for acceleration.
rubric.description: Defines acceleration as the rate of change of velocity with time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.description: Writes the SI unit of acceleration.

modelAnswer: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with time.
Its SI unit is metre per second squared (m/s²).

items.followUp: State Hooke's law and the condition under which it is valid.

rubric.why: States the proportional relationship between applied force and extension.
rubric.description: Says that extension is directly proportional to the applied force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct proportionality.

rubric.why: Includes the condition for the law to hold.
rubric.description: States that the law holds provided the elastic limit is not exceeded.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the elastic-limit condition.

modelAnswer: Hooke's law states that the extension of an elastic body is directly proportional to the applied force, provided its elastic limit is not exceeded.

items.followUp: What must be true about the resultant force on a body in translational equilibrium?

rubric.why: Gives the force condition for equilibrium.
rubric.description: States that the resultant (net) force on the body is zero.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for zero resultant force.

rubric.why: Describes the body's motion when the equilibrium condition holds.
rubric.description: States that the body has no acceleration (it remains at rest or moves with constant velocity).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for zero acceleration or an equivalent motion description.

modelAnswer: A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force acting on it is zero.
Therefore, it has no acceleration and remains at rest or moves with constant velocity.

items.followUp: Give one example each of a renewable and a non-renewable energy source.

rubric.why: Defines a renewable source or identifies a valid example.
rubric.description: States that renewable sources are naturally replenished, or gives a valid example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition or a valid example such as sunlight, wind, or water.

rubric.why: Defines a non-renewable source or identifies a valid example.
rubric.description: States that non-renewable sources are finite or are not naturally replenished on a human timescale, or gives a valid example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition or a valid example such as coal, oil, or natural gas.

modelAnswer: Renewable sources of energy are naturally replenished and can be used repeatedly, for example sunlight and wind.
Non-renewable sources are finite and are not replenished on a human timescale, for example coal and oil.

items.followUp: Name the device in a power station that generates electricity from the rotation of a turbine.

rubric.why: Names a device that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the correct device.

modelAnswer: A generator (or dynamo) converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.

items.followUp: State one difference between heat and temperature, including their SI units.

rubric.why: Distinguishes heat from temperature by their meanings.
rubric.description: Identifies heat as energy transferred due to a temperature difference and temperature as a measure of hotness (or average kinetic energy).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct distinction in meaning.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the SI units of heat and temperature.
rubric.description: Gives joule (J) for heat and kelvin (K) for temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct units.

modelAnswer: Heat is energy transferred from a hotter body to a colder body because of a temperature difference; its SI unit is joule (J).
Temperature is a measure of the degree of hotness of a body (related to the average kinetic energy of its particles); its SI unit is kelvin (K).

items.followUp: Two masses of 6 kg and 4 kg are connected by a light string over a frictionless pulley. Find their acceleration and the tension in the string. Take g = 9.8 m/s².

rubric.why: Sets up Newton's second-law equations for the two masses.
rubric.description: Writes the equations of motion for the heavier mass moving down and the lighter mass moving up.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct equations of motion.

rubric.why: Derives the acceleration for the two-mass system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula.
Award 1 mark for the correct formula.

rubric.why: Identifies the direction of motion consistent with the assumed mass ordering.
rubric.description: States that the heavier mass moves downward and the lighter mass moves upward.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct directions, with the heavier mass identified as m1.

modelAnswer: Let the masses be m₁ and m₂, with m₁ > m₂; m₁ moves downward and m₂ moves upward.
For m₁: given mass = m₁ kg; weight = m₁g N; equation of motion: m₁g − T = m₁a.
For m₂: given mass = m₂ kg; equation of motion: T − m₂g = m₂a.
Therefore, acceleration: a = [(m₁ − m₂)/(m₁ + m₂)]g m/s².
Substituting this into either equation of motion gives tension: T = [2m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂)]g N.
